Based on the specific data you provided, the short answer is: **It is highly unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with the naked eye right now.**

Here is the breakdown of why you can probably breathe a sigh of relief:

### 1. The "Daylight" Factor
You mentioned the sky brightness is "bright daylight." In astronomy, the human eye struggles to perceive celestial bodies against a bright blue sky because the atmosphere scatters so much sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). For a celestial object to be visible during the day, it generally needs to be very large or very bright (like Venus or a Full Moon).

### 2. The Phase (Illumination)
The Moon is only **1.32% illuminated**. This means it is in a "New Moon" phase. Even though it is physically above the horizon, it is essentially a dark disc. It is not reflecting enough sunlight to create a visible "glow" against the bright daytime sky.

### 3. Proximity to the Sun
The Moon is only **13.169 degrees** away from the Sun. While this means it is physically in the same general area of the sky, it also means it is sitting in the brightest part of the atmosphere. The glare from the Sun (which is at a low altitude of 5 degrees) will wash out almost anything nearby.

### 4. The "Contrast" Problem
Because the Moon is so thin (1.32%) and the Sun is so close, the Moon will be "lost" in the solar glare. To see it, you would likely need high-powered binoculars or a telescope to pick out the tiny sliver of light, but even then, the glare from the Sun would make it very difficult.

**Verdict:** 
Since you are looking at a nearly invisible sliver of a Moon in the middle of a bright day, **you almost certainly won't see it.** You can rest easy!
